title: 18. Effects of timing of mineral drench administration on performance and mineral status of grazing beef calves.
content:
Abstract
In grazing systems, forages serve as the primary source of minerals. However, forages may contain inadequate concentrations to meet cattle requirements, requiring supplementation programs. Nursing calves are particularly vulnerable to trace mineral deficiencies, especially during stressful periods such as weaning, transportation, and commingling. Single-use, pulse-dose products can be an alternative to boost their status at those specific events. The use of oral drenches as additional supplementation has recently gained popularity due to their convenience and capacity to provide trace minerals at strategic intervals. Therefore, it was hypothesized that providing a trace mineral drench at different time points would be an effective strategy to improve the trace mineral status of calves and subsequent performance at and post-weaning. Thus, the objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of a trace mineral drench that provides Co, Cu, Mn, Se, and Zn, along with vitamin E, at strategic intervals. Sixty crossbred (Angus x Hereford) calves were selected from the herd of Eastern Oregon Agricultural Research Center (EOARC). Calves were selected during their dams’ breeding season and were randomly allocated into 1 of 4 treatments: 1) Control, no drench administration; 2) Breeding, with drench provided at breeding; 3) Weaning, with drench provided at weaning; and 4) Breeding + Weaning, with drench provided at breeding and again at weaning. Drench was provided according to the manufacturer’s recommendation at 5 ml/45 kg of body weight (BW). Liver samples (n = 23) and BW were collected from calves at drench administration throughout the study. After weaning, calves were preconditioned for 45 days, and a final BW and a liver sample were collected at the end of the preconditioning. Preliminary data for BW and mineral status were analyzed using MIXED procedures of SAS (SAS Inc., Cary, NC, USA). Statistical significance was set at a P ≤ 0.05. No effects of treatment (P ≥ 0.67) were observed for calf BW at any of the time points where BW was recorded (113 ± 5 kg; 225 ± 9 kg; 250 ± 9 kg breeding, weaning, and end of preconditioning, respectively). Of the trace minerals evaluated, a tendency for treatment effect (P = 0.08) was observed for Cu status of calves at weaning, where calves assigned to receive drench at breeding tended to have or had greater (P ≤ 0.06) Cu status at weaning than calves assigned to all other treatments (21, 53, 27, and, 42 ± 12 mg/kg for Control, Breeding, Weaning, and Breeding + Weaning treatments, respectively). Although no effects were observed for calf growth, the use of drench at the dam’s breeding can be a convenient alternative to enhance the Cu status of calves at weaning, especially in systems with low Cu concentrations.
